blocks.title: Networks
blocks.md: A **network** is a group of computers connected to share data and resources. A **LAN** covers a small area (a school lab). A **WAN** covers a large area (towns, countries); the **Internet** is a worldwide network of networks. Parts: **router**, **switch**, network cable or **Wi-Fi**, **network interface card**.

blocks.title: Topologies
blocks.md: **Star**: every computer connects to a central switch (easy to add/remove; if the centre fails everything stops). **Bus**: one shared cable. **Ring**: computers joined in a loop. The star is the most common in schools and offices.

blocks.caption: Four devices each connected to a central switch.
blocks.alt: Star topology: PC 1, PC 2, PC 3 and a printer all connected to a central switch.

blocks.title: Internet and web
blocks.md: The **Internet** is the network; the **World Wide Web** is the collection of web pages on it. A **browser** shows pages. A **URL** is the address of a page. An **ISP** gives Internet access. **Email** sends messages using an address such as name@example.com.

blocks.title: Download time
blocks.md: Data rates are in **bits** per second (bps); files are in **bytes**. Time (s) = file size in bits / speed in bits per second. 1 byte = 8 bits.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The Internet is **not** the same as the Web.
- Mbps (megabits per second) is not MB/s (megabytes per second): divide Mbps by 8 to get MB/s.
- In a star network the failure of one cable affects only that computer.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Download time
blocks.statement: A 24 MB file is downloaded at 8 Mbps (megabits per second). How long does it take?

blocks.title: Example 2 - Choose a network
blocks.statement: A school with two buildings in Bafoussam wants to link its labs. Name the network type for one lab and for the link to a bank across town.
steps: One lab in one building is a small area: LAN.
A link over a larger distance between sites/organisations is a WAN.
blocks.answer: LAN for the lab; WAN for the long link.

blocks.title: Threats
blocks.md: **Malware** is harmful software: **viruses** attach to files and spread; **worms** spread by themselves; **spyware** secretly collects information. **Phishing** uses fake emails or messages to trick people into giving passwords or money. **Hacking** is unauthorised access to a system.

blocks.title: Protection
blocks.md: Use **strong passwords** (long, mixed letters, numbers and symbols, different for each account), keep software **updated**, install **antivirus**, use a **firewall**, **back up** files regularly, and do not open unknown attachments or links. Log out on shared computers.

blocks.caption: A two-column table matching each threat to a protection measure.
blocks.alt: Table: virus - antivirus; hacking - passwords and firewall; phishing - check the sender; data loss - backups.

blocks.title: Email safety and ethics
blocks.md: Do not share passwords or personal details; check the sender before you click; do not forward chain messages. **Copyright** protects creators: you may not copy or sell others' work without permission. Be respectful online; **cyberbullying** is harmful.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Antivirus does not remove the need to be careful.
- Using the same password everywhere is dangerous.
- Being offered easy money by email is a typical sign of fraud.
- A backup stored only on the same computer is not safe.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Spot the phishing
blocks.statement: An email says: Your account will close! Send your password to keep it. What should you do?
steps: The message creates fear and asks for a password: signs of phishing.
Never reply; do not click links; delete it and report to the real service by its official contact.
blocks.answer: Treat it as phishing and do not respond.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Strong password
blocks.statement: Which is stronger: buea123 or T7#mQ!2rv9? Explain.
steps: buea123 is short and easy to guess (a town plus numbers).
T7#mQ!2rv9 is long with mixed upper and lower case, digits and symbols.
